 Proposal: Late tax bills could extend Allegheny County payment deadlines
Allegheny County proposal aims to protect tax discounts when bills arrive late
 By Megan Trotter 2 Min Read 
 • Nov. 4, 2026 
 | 12 hours ago 
-->
 Go Ad-Free today 
 Allegheny County Councilman Dan Grzybek, D-Bethel Park, at a county council meeting in downtown Pittsburgh last month. (Massoud Hossaini | TribLive) 
 Allegheny County Councilman Dan Grzybek wants to improve transparency and fairness in the county’s real estate tax process.
 On Tuesday, Gryzbek proposed adding a Tax Bill Disclosure Bill of Rights to the county’s existing county code that would require the County Treasurer’s Office to mail, email and make property tax bills available online by the end of January each year.
 The ordinance would establish standardized billing retirement aimed at ensuring taxpayers received clear information about property assessments, tax rates, total amounts owed, payment deadlines, discounts and penalties.
 “The goal really is to make sure that we’re doing things like making sure folks are getting as much time as possible with their tax bills,” said Gryzbek, D-Bethel Park. “They’re getting their tax bills as early as possible — that things are clearly displayed on their tax bill.”
 Part of the measure would protect taxpayers from losing the 2% early-payment discount when the county fails to issue tax bills on time. If passed, the legislation would extend discount deadlines by 60 days if an individual’s bill is not available by Jan. 31.
 The 60 days would begin after the bill becomes available, while the full-payment deadline would extend to 90 days.
 The ordinance would also allow taxpayers to request written payment of receipts.
 “A lot of, especially our older folks in Allegheny County, they’re used to getting that written receipt for whatever they’re kind of filing their paperwork and keeping their records, and it was something that we got rid of because we largely computerized and digitized all of these records,” Gryzbek said.
 Under the provisions, the treasurer would be required to notify the county executive, county council president and the public within two business days of missing the deadline, in addition to providing an estimated date for when the bills will become available.
 Allegheny County Director of Tax and Licensing Michael Horvath advocated on behalf of the treasurer’s office.
 Horvath said the legislation would help make the county’s real estate tax collection process more efficient and responsive to residents.
 “By codifying these practices, we can establish clear expectations, provide greater consistency and predictability for taxpayers, and make sure that these improvements continue into the future,” Horvath said.
 The legislation was referred to the Committee on Government Reform.
